name: Tamil
info: Tamil is a Dravidian language of the Tamil people of southern India and northern and eastern Sri Lanka, attested since about 300 BCE, one of the longest-surviving classical languages in the world, with the Sangam poems among its early works.

facts.family: Dravidian, southern branch; descended from Proto-Dravidian, most likely spoken around the third millennium BCE. Its closest major relative is Malayalam, which began to diverge around the 9th century CE.
facts.script: Tamil-Brahmi in its earliest inscriptions; later vaṭṭeḻuttu, alongside Grantha and Pallava, until the present Tamil script: 12 vowels, 18 consonants and the āytam, 247 characters in all, with six Grantha letters for borrowed sounds.
facts.earliest: Short inscriptions in Tamil-Brahmi, attested since c. 300 BCE; earlier dates are claimed for writing on burial urns at Adichanallur (from at least 696 BCE) and a Keezhadi sample (around 580 BCE). The earliest long text is the Tolkāppiyam, whose oldest layers may date to the late 2nd century BCE.
facts.status: Living: spoken by the Tamil people in Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and northern and eastern Sri Lanka and by communities worldwide; official in Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, an official language of Sri Lanka and Singapore, and in 2004 the first recognised classical language of India.

t: Tamil is a Dravidian language attested since about 300 BCE in Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions, and one of the longest-surviving classical languages in the world.

Its early literature includes the Tolkāppiyam, the oldest Tamil grammar, and the 2,381 Sangam poems, dated between the 1st century BCE and the 5th century CE; Tamil inscriptions have been found as far away as Sri Lanka, Thailand and Egypt.

Old Tamil became Middle Tamil by the 8th century and Modern Tamil from 1600; today Tamil is official in Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Sri Lanka and Singapore, and in 2004 it became the first recognised classical language of India.
dyk: Scholars trace the English word rice to Tamil arici, through loans from the Tamil of 400 BCE into Hebrew and then into Greek óruza.
ev: Old Tamil appears in short inscriptions in Tamil-Brahmi, a variant of the Brahmi script
The Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela, king of Kalinga, names a Tamira Samghatta, a Tamil confederacy
Egyptian pottery of this date found at Quseir al-Qadim, likely the port of Myos Hormos, bears Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions

The Naṉṉūl restates the rules of the Tolkāppiyam and becomes the standard grammar of literary Tamil
Portuguese missionaries print the prayer book Thambiran Vanakkam, making Tamil the first Indian language to be printed and published
The Pure Tamil Movement campaigns to remove Sanskrit elements from Tamil
Tamil becomes the first legally recognised classical language of India

sections.origins:
Tamil belongs to the southern branch of the Dravidian languages, a family of around 26 languages native to the Indian subcontinent. Like the others it descends from Proto-Dravidian, which was most likely spoken around the third millennium BCE, possibly around the lower Godavari river basin, by people of the Neolithic cultures of South India. Its closest major relative is Malayalam, and Kannada too is relatively close. Hindu legend tells that Tamil, as Tamil Thāi, “Mother Tamil”, was created by Shiva and brought to the people by Murugan and the sage Agastya.

The language is attested since about 300 BCE. Its earliest records are short inscriptions in Tamil-Brahmi, a variant of the Brahmi script, and earlier dates have been claimed: burial urns found at Adichanallur in 2004, dating from at least 696 BCE, carry writing in Tamil-Brahmi, and a sample from Keezhadi has been claimed to date to around 580 BCE. Apparent Tamil loanwords in Biblical Hebrew from before 500 BCE are the oldest attestation of all.

The origin of the name is unclear. The Tolkāppiyam is the earliest text to use it, and around 150 BCE the Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela, the Jain king of Kalinga, names a Tamira Samghatta, a Tamil confederacy. Scholars have read tamiḻ as “our own speech” or “self-speak”, and the Tamil Lexicon of the University of Madras defines it as “sweetness”.
sections.structure:
The Tamil script descends from Tamil-Brahmi, by way of a script called vaṭṭeḻuttu used alongside Grantha and Pallava. It has 12 vowels, 18 consonants and one special character, the āytam, which combine into 247 characters. As in other Indic scripts, every consonant carries a built-in vowel a: a dot called the puḷḷi removes it, so that ன is ṉa and ன் is ṉ. The script does not tell voiced from unvoiced stops, which are voiced by their place in the word, and six letters from the Grantha script are sometimes used for sounds borrowed from Sanskrit and other languages.

Tamil grammar is agglutinative: suffixes are added to a root, one after another, to mark class, number, case, tense and other categories, with no fixed limit. The single word pōkamuṭiyātavarkaḷukkāka means “for the sake of those who cannot go”. Nouns fall into two great classes, the “rational”, humans and gods, and the “irrational”, everything else, with five classes in all. Traditional grammarians counted eight cases on the Sanskrit model; modern grammarians treat each suffix as a case of its own.

The verb comes at the end of the clause, in the order subject–object–verb, and Tamil uses postpositions rather than prepositions. It has no articles and no linking verb “is”, so atu eṉ vīṭu means “that [is] my house”, and it tells an inclusive “we”, nām, from an exclusive one, nāṅkaḷ. Even its terms for grammar are Tamil rather than Sanskrit.
sections.speakers:
Tamil is the main language of most people in Tamil Nadu and Puducherry in India and in the Northern and Eastern Provinces of Sri Lanka, and small minorities speak it in other Indian states and in Colombo and the Sri Lankan hill country. It once reached further: Tamil or its dialects were the major language of administration, literature and daily life in Kerala until the 12th century CE, and Tamil inscriptions were made in southern Andhra Pradesh until then and in southern Karnataka from the 10th to the 14th centuries.

Tamil also travelled by sea. It was the lingua franca of early maritime traders from India, and Tamil inscriptions in Brahmi have been found in Sri Lanka and on trade goods in Thailand and Egypt. Migrants of the colonial era took it to Malaysia, Singapore, Mauritius, South Africa, Burma and other lands; in Réunion, Guyana, Fiji and Trinidad many have Tamil origins but few speak it, and in Réunion, where France forbade it in public, it is now being learnt again. Malaysia has 543 government primary schools that teach in Tamil.

Today Tamil is official in Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and is one of the 22 languages of the eighth schedule of India’s constitution. It is an official and national language of Sri Lanka, with Sinhala, and an official language of Singapore, and migrants from Sri Lanka and India speak it in Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia.
sections.literature:
The earliest Tamil literary works and their commentaries praise the Pandiyan kings for organising the Tamil Sangams, long-lasting academies that worked on the language. The oldest surviving text is the Tolkāppiyam, a work on Tamil grammar and poetics whose oldest layers could be as old as the late 2nd century BCE. It describes much of Tamil grammar in five parts, eḻuttu, col, poruḷ, yāppu and aṇi, the last two mostly for poetry.

Beside it stands Sangam literature, a corpus of 2,381 poems usually dated between the 1st century BCE and the 5th century CE. In the Tevaram of Cuntaramurti the poet asks Shiva, “Do you know proper Tamil?”; the scholar David Shulman reads the question as one about knowing how to love, and notes that to “know Tamil” could also mean to be a civilised being. In the 9th and 10th centuries a special form of Tamil, the Vaishnava paribasai, grew up to express Vaishnavite religious values. In the 13th century the Naṉṉūl restated and clarified the rules of the Tolkāppiyam, and it remains the standard grammar of literary Tamil.

Tamil was early in print. In 1578 Portuguese Christian missionaries published a prayer book in the old Tamil script, Thambiran Vanakkam, making Tamil the first Indian language to be printed and published, and the Tamil Lexicon of the University of Madras was one of the earliest dictionaries of an Indian language. A 2001 survey counted 1,863 Tamil newspapers, 353 of them dailies.
sections.change:
Scholars divide the history of Tamil into Old Tamil (300 BCE–700 CE), Middle Tamil (700–1600) and Modern Tamil (from 1600). The change from Old to Middle Tamil, complete by the 8th century, brought the near disappearance of the old sound written with the āytam (ஃ), the merging of two n sounds and the turning of a stop into an r-like sound. Above all, a present tense appeared, grown from the verb kil, “to be possible”, which in Old Tamil had marked short-lived actions and became the present marker kiṉṟa.

Written Tamil still follows the Middle Tamil of the 13th-century Naṉṉūl, and it is conservative enough to read eighth-century inscriptions with, while the spoken language has moved on, losing the negative conjugation of verbs and some vowels between consonants. Tamil lives in diglossia, with high and low registers: classical caṅkattamiḻ, the formal centamiḻ of textbooks and public speaking, and the colloquial koṭuntamiḻ of cinema, television and many politicians, often mixed with English in cities as Tanglish.

Dialects grew from different sound changes: the classical iṅku, “here”, is iṅkū in the Kongu dialect of Coimbatore, inga in Thanjavur and iṅkai in parts of Sri Lanka. Sri Lankan Tamil keeps words no longer used in India and has borrowed from Portuguese, Dutch and English, and castes have sociolects of their own, among them Brahmin Tamil. Malayalam, which began to diverge in the 9th century, had become a separate language by the 13th or 14th.
sections.legacy:
Tamil has lent words far beyond India. Besides rice, English has cheroot from curuṭṭu, “rolled up”, mango from māṅgāy, mulligatawny from miḷaku taṇṇīr, “pepper water”, curry from kaṟi, catamaran from kaṭṭu maram, “bundled logs”, and congee from kañji, and anaconda may come from anaikkonda, “having killed an elephant”. Tamil in turn took words from its trading partners, such as cavvarici, “sago”, from Malay and campān, “skiff”, from Chinese, and later from Urdu, Portuguese, French and English.

Its vocabulary is mainly Dravidian, and it was never as heavily Sanskritised as the other Dravidian languages: complex ideas in science, art, religion and law could always be expressed without Sanskrit loans. Some late medieval authors resisted Sanskritisation, and in the 20th century the Pure Tamil Movement, taṉit tamiḻ iyakkam, led by Parithimaar Kalaignar and Maraimalai Adigal and supported by Dravidian parties, replaced many Sanskrit words; by some estimates their share in formal Tamil fell from 40–50% to about 20%. Learned bodies have coined technical terms from Tamil roots, and by 2019 the listed vocabulary held over 470,000 words.

In 2004, after a campaign by Tamil associations, Tamil became the first legally recognised classical language of India, announced by President Abdul Kalam, himself a Tamil. Canada keeps January as Tamil Heritage Month, and South Africa’s constitution protects the language.

summary: Tamil is a Dravidian language attested since about 300 BCE, spoken by the Tamil people of southern India and Sri Lanka and by communities across the world. The Tolkāppiyam and the Sangam poems stand at the start of its well-documented literary history, and words such as curry, mango and catamaran passed from it into English. In 2004 it became the first recognised classical language of India.
notes: References: the saved article’s References, Bibliography and Further reading sections are empty, so none are listed.
Speakers: the article gives no total number of Tamil speakers anywhere, so status has no figure. Worth adding from another source if the editor wants one.

Start -300 (circa): the lede’s “attested since c. 300 BCE” and Old Tamil from 300 BCE / the 3rd century BCE. The article also claims older dates (Adichanallur urns with Tamil-Brahmi writing “dating from at least 696 BCE”; a Keezhadi sample “claimed to be dated to around 580 BCE”; Tamil loanwords in Biblical Hebrew “before 500 BCE, the oldest attestation of the language”). These are given hedged, not used for the start.

Inconsistencies in the article: Old Tamil is “300 BCE–700 CE” in one place and “3rd century BCE to the 8th century CE” in another; the Tolkāppiyam is “as early as the 2nd century BCE” and “as old as the late 2nd century BCE”; the Sangam corpus is “over 2,000 poems” in the lede and “2,381 poems” later (I used 2,381). The rice loan is dated “400 BCE”, the Hebrew loanwords “before 500 BCE”.
2004: the legal status for classical languages was created “in October 2004”, yet the recognition was announced by President Abdul Kalam on 6 June 2004. I gave only the year.

The 1st-century BCE event: the article says “Egyptian pottery dating back to first century BCE with ancient Tamil Brahmi inscriptions” was found in 2007 at Quseir al-Qadim; I did not say who wrote the inscriptions.
Literature is thin in the article: no named Sangam poets or anthologies, no Tirukkural, Silappatikaram or Kamba Ramayanam, no dates for Cuntaramurti or the Tevaram. Left out for that reason.
Left out: the ASI count of inscriptions (about 60,000 of 100,000 in Tamil Nadu), Haryana’s nominal official status, the Karachi community, and the phonology tables.
